record.paper_title: Whitehead's Asphericity Question and Its Relation to Other Open Problems
record.original_question: Does every finitely generated perfect group have a single normal generator?

evidence.quote: a finitely generated perfect group has a single normal generator

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called perfect if it equals its own commutator subgroup, i.e., $G = [G,G]$. An element $g \in G$ is called a normal generator of $G$ if the smallest normal subgroup of $G$ containing $g$ is all of $G$; equivalently, $G$ is the normal closure $\langle\!\langle g \rangle\!\rangle^G$. The normal rank of $G$ is the minimum cardinality of a subset $S \subseteq G$ whose normal closure equals $G$.

Question (Wiegold): Does every finitely generated perfect group admit a single normal generator? In other words, is it true that for every finitely generated group $G$ with $G = [G,G]$, there exists an element $g \in G$ such that $G$ is the normal closure of $\{g\}$?
artifact.status_search_result: A 2025 preprint by Chen and Heuer ("The Wiegold problem and free products of left-orderable groups", arXiv:2510.26073) announces a negative solution to Wiegold's problem: they prove that any free product of nontrivial left-orderable groups has normal rank greater than one, and combining this with the existence of finitely generated perfect left-orderable groups yields finitely generated perfect groups that are not normally generated by a single element. Prior to this, the problem (posed by Wiegold in 1976) had been considered open.

status_evidence.title: The Wiegold problem and free products of left-orderable groups
status_evidence.snippet: Any free product of nontrivial left-orderable groups has normal rank greater than one; this solves the Wiegold problem by taking free products of finitely generated perfect left-orderable groups.
status_evidence.claim: Recent preprint resolves Wiegold's problem in the negative.

status_evidence.title: Finitely Presented Groups (problem list)
status_evidence.snippet: Wiegold's question on whether every finitely generated perfect group has a single normal generator was listed as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Long-standing status as an open problem prior to 2025.
